mcqs.question: A hot path allocates a small temporary object on every iteration, run a million times per second. Beyond the direct cost of allocating, what's the other cost this creates?
options: Every one of those objects is something the garbage collector will eventually have to trace to determine reachability, increasing collection frequency and duration
None — in managed languages, allocation has no cost beyond the initial memory write
The objects permanently increase the process's minimum memory footprint even after being collected
The allocations bypass the garbage collector entirely since they are short-lived
mcqs.explanation: Allocation cost isn't paid once at creation — each allocated object is something the collector must eventually trace, so a high allocation rate directly increases how often GC runs and how much work each cycle does. Short-lived objects are still traced by young-gen collections; they aren't exempt.

mcqs.question: Why do generational garbage collectors split the heap into a young generation and an old generation?
options: To allow the two generations to be collected on entirely separate CPU cores simultaneously
Because most objects die young, so scanning a small young generation frequently is cheap, while the larger old generation — mostly live data — is scanned only rarely
Because old objects are inherently larger in memory footprint than young objects
To eliminate the need for stop-the-world pauses entirely
mcqs.explanation: The generational split is based on the empirical observation that most objects die young — so frequent, cheap young-gen collections handle the common case, while the old generation (mostly long-lived, reachable data) is scanned only occasionally since a full scan there is far more expensive. Generational GC does not eliminate stop-the-world pauses; it just keeps most of them short.

mcqs.question: A batch job that only cares about total completion time, versus a service with a strict p99 latency SLO — how should their GC tuning differ?
options: Both should use identical GC settings since tuning only affects total memory usage, not latency
The service should disable GC entirely to guarantee no pauses

The batch job should tune toward a larger heap and fewer, larger pauses for higher throughput, while the latency-sensitive service should tune toward smaller, more frequent, more predictable pauses even at some throughput cost
The batch job should use the smallest possible heap to minimize memory usage, regardless of pause frequency
mcqs.explanation: GC tuning is a real trade-off between throughput and pause time — a batch job with no latency SLO benefits from a larger heap and fewer, more expensive pauses since only total time matters, while a service with a tail-latency SLO needs smaller, more predictable pauses even if that costs some overall throughput.

mcqs.question: An application in a garbage-collected language shows heap usage steadily climbing over days under steady traffic, even though GC cycles still run and reclaim some memory each time. What does this indicate?
options: The garbage collector itself is malfunctioning and failing to run correctly
This is normal behavior for any long-running managed-language process and requires no investigation

The application's code is retaining references to objects it no longer needs — a growing unbounded cache, unregistered listeners, or a static collection — that the GC correctly considers still reachable
The heap size limit was configured too low and needs to be increased
mcqs.explanation: A GC only reclaims unreachable objects — if application code still holds a reference, the collector correctly leaves it alone no matter how long it's actually needed. Steady heap growth with GC still running normally is the signature of exactly this: a leak caused by retained references, not a GC malfunction.

mcqs.question: A high-throughput network server pools and reuses byte buffers instead of allocating a fresh one per request. Beyond the direct allocation cost saved, what specific GC benefit does this provide?
options: It reduces the total number of objects the collector has to trace, which can meaningfully lower how often any GC pause — young or old generation — occurs at all
It eliminates the need for a young generation entirely
It guarantees the application will never experience a stop-the-world pause
It converts all remaining allocations into off-heap memory automatically
mcqs.explanation: Pooling reduces the raw number of objects the collector must eventually trace — at high allocation rates this can be the difference between the young generation filling up (triggering a collection) every few milliseconds versus every few seconds, directly cutting overall GC pause frequency, not just per-allocation cost.

mcqs.question: A team eliminates visible GC pauses by setting the heap size enormous so garbage collection rarely runs. What is the real cost of this approach?
options: There is no real cost — a sufficiently large heap genuinely eliminates the need to ever collect garbage
The eventual full GC, or an out-of-memory crash, that occurs once the enormous heap finally fills — a pause far worse than the ones that were 'fixed', scaling with however large the heap grew
The application will consume less total memory than before, since collections are less frequent
This approach only affects throughput, with no impact on tail latency whatsoever
mcqs.explanation: Deferring GC by growing the heap doesn't remove the underlying allocation rate — it defers the cost to a single, much larger eventual pause (or an OOM crash) that scales with the heap size. The actual fix is reducing allocation rate and fixing real leaks, not delaying the reckoning to a worse moment.
